unit.title: Reading a trail description
unit.summary: Miles, gain, grade, pace and the vocabulary of difficulty.

lessons.title: Miles are not the whole story
lessons.objective: You can explain why elevation gain matters as much as distance.

payload.prompt: A 6-mile hike with 2,000 ft of gain feels like about how many flat miles?

explanation.correct: A common rule of thumb adds one mile of effort for every 500 feet of gain. Two thousand feet adds about four, so 6 miles feels like roughly 10 flat miles.
explanation.incorrect: Elevation gain multiplies effort. Adding about a mile of effort per 500 feet of climbing turns 6 miles with 2,000 feet into roughly 10 flat-mile equivalents.

payload.prompt: Two hikes: 6 miles flat, or 4 miles with 3,000 ft of gain. Which usually takes longer?

options.text: The 4-mile hike with 3,000 ft of gain
They take about the same time
Impossible to compare without knowing terrain

explanation.correct: The steep one. By Naismith's rule, 6 flat miles take about 2 hours, while 4 miles plus 3,000 feet of gain takes about 1.3 plus 1.5, nearly 3 hours.
explanation.incorrect: Gain is the hidden variable. Distance alone does not tell the story: the shorter, steeper hike takes longer.
explanation.sayThisLine: Only four miles? What is the elevation gain? That changes everything.

payload.prompt: A trail climbs 500 ft in half a mile. Is this steep?

options.text: Not steep at all, just a casual climb

explanation.correct: That is about a 19% grade: 500 ft of rise over 2,640 ft (half a mile) of horizontal distance. It is steep enough to feel in your quads.
explanation.incorrect: Grade is rise over run. Five hundred feet in half a mile is about 19 percent: expect a grinding climb and tired legs.
explanation.sayThisLine: The trail climbs five hundred feet in half a mile. This is going to be steep.

payload.prompt: A trail listing says 8 miles with 800 ft gain. How many hours?

explanation.correct: Naismith's rule: 8 miles at 3 mph is about 2.7 hours, plus 800 ft of gain at 2,000 ft per hour is 0.4 hours. That is about 3 hours moving. Add breaks and plan for 3.5 to 4.
explanation.incorrect: Use Naismith's rule: one hour per three miles, plus one hour per 2,000 feet of gain. Eight miles is about 2.7 hours, plus 0.4 hours for the gain.

payload.prompt: Is elevation gain already built into the mileage number?

scene.alt: A trail description listing 6 miles and 3,000 feet of gain as two separate numbers.

choices.label: No, it is a separate key number

explanation.correct: Distance and gain are independent. Gain tells you how much climbing to expect, so two hikes of equal mileage can be totally different days.
explanation.incorrect: Six miles with 3,000 feet is a slog; six miles with 200 feet is a cruise. Mileage alone hides the climbing.
explanation.sayThisLine: The gain is the number that actually tells you how hard it is.

lessons.title: How steep is steep
lessons.objective: You can turn rise and run into a grade and feel what it means.

payload.prompt: A hillside climbs 100 ft in 400 ft horizontal distance. What percent grade?

explanation.correct: Grade = (rise ÷ run) × 100. Here: (100 ÷ 400) × 100 = 25%. That's steep; your breathing gets hard.
explanation.incorrect: Grade is the ratio of vertical rise to horizontal distance. 100 feet up over 400 feet horizontal = 25 percent grade.

payload.prompt: Which section is steeper?

diagram.alt: Two slopes: left gradual, right steep.

explanation.correct: The right covers more vertical in the same space. That's steeper.
explanation.incorrect: Grade is the climb angle. The right rises sharply—higher grade, harder.

payload.prompt: A 10% grade trail: roughly how much elevation in one mile?

explanation.correct: One mile = 5,280 feet. Ten percent grade means 0.10 × 5,280 = 528 feet of elevation. That's noticeable but not extreme.
explanation.incorrect: Grade × horizontal distance = elevation. A 10% grade over a mile (5,280 horizontal feet) equals about 528 vertical feet.

payload.prompt: Order these grades from easiest to hardest on your legs.

items.why: Barely noticeable, like a gentle rise.
Steep enough to have you breathing hard.
Very steep, and a grind on any trail.

explanation.correct: Lower percent means gentler slope. Three percent is barely noticeable; twenty-five percent will make your legs burn.
explanation.incorrect: Grade is rise over run, so a bigger percentage is steeper. Line them up from gentlest to steepest.

payload.prompt: You read a trail climbs 1,500 ft in 2 miles. Approximately what's the average grade?

explanation.correct: Two miles = 10,560 horizontal feet. (1,500 ÷ 10,560) × 100 = 14% average. That's sustained climbing, expect to work.
explanation.incorrect: Do the math: 1,500 ft rise over two miles (10,560 ft horizontal) is a 14% average grade. That's moderately steep.

lessons.title: Planning with Naismith
lessons.objective: You can estimate hiking time from distance and gain.

payload.prompt: A trail is 9 miles with 1,200 ft gain. How long by Naismith?

explanation.correct: Naismith: 9 miles at 3 mph is 3 hours, plus 1,200 ft at 2,000 ft per hour is 0.6 hours. That is about 3.6 hours of moving time, before breaks.
explanation.incorrect: Use the rule: 1 hour per 3 miles, plus 1 hour per 2,000 feet of gain. Nine miles is 3 hours, 1,200 feet is 0.6 hours, so about 3.5 hours before breaks.

payload.prompt: Complete Naismith's rule.
payload.template: {{one}} hour per {{three}} miles, plus {{one2}} hour per 2,000 feet of gain.

explanation.correct: That is Naismith's rule: distance and gain set your baseline time.
explanation.incorrect: One hour per three miles plus one hour per 2,000 feet of climbing.

payload.prompt: 4 hours moving time by Naismith. Add time for breaks, lunch and photos. Total?

explanation.correct: Real-world hiking adds contingency. Add 30% to 50% to Naismith time for breaks, lunch, photos and slower real pace. Four hours becomes 5 to 6 hours.
explanation.incorrect: Moving time is just walking. Total time includes stops for food, water, views and photos. Most hikers add 30 to 50 percent.

payload.prompt: Naismith assumes a hiking speed of roughly how many miles per hour on flat terrain?

explanation.correct: Naismith's baseline is 3 mph on flat ground, a sustainable pace for a fit hiker. Steeper terrain, heavy packs or tired legs slow you down.
explanation.incorrect: The rule uses 3 mph as the baseline on flat terrain. That is neither power-hiking nor strolling—a real-world pace most people can sustain.

payload.prompt: Your plan says 3.5 hours moving time. You leave at 7 AM. When do you plan to return?

options.text: 11:30 AM to 12:30 PM, realistic pace with breaks
Impossible to say without knowing the terrain

explanation.correct: Add 30 to 50 percent to moving time for lunch, water stops, photos and slower stretches. Three and a half hours moving becomes about 4.5 to 5.25 hours, so back around noon.
explanation.incorrect: Moving time is not total time. You will stop for food, water and the view, so add 30 to 50 percent, and keep a cushion before dark.

lessons.title: Real pace, fantasy pace
lessons.objective: You can adjust pace for terrain, pack and group.

payload.prompt: On steep, rocky terrain, average pace drops to roughly what?

explanation.correct: Steep, rough terrain cuts pace in half or more: 1 to 1.5 mph is realistic. Your feet work harder, rocks slow you, and you rest more often.
explanation.incorrect: Terrain matters hugely. Rocky slopes, scree and steep grades drop pace from 3 mph (flat) to 1 to 1.5 mph or slower.

payload.prompt: Which usually slows a hiker's pace the most?

options.text: All of the above, roughly equally

explanation.correct: Rock scrambles and scree stop you cold. You move one step at a time, carefully. Gain slows pace, but rough terrain slows it more.
explanation.incorrect: Difficult terrain—scree, boulders, rock scrambles—is the biggest pace killer. Even fitter hikers slow to one step at a time.
explanation.sayThisLine: We did a section of scree and dropped to a mile per hour or less.

payload.prompt: Around 8,000 ft, a fit hiker's pace is roughly what percent of sea-level pace?

explanation.correct: Thinner air makes hard effort harder. At 8,000 feet most people slow modestly, to roughly 85 to 95 percent of sea-level pace, and more the higher they go.
explanation.incorrect: Altitude slows everyone a bit. Around 8,000 feet expect a modest drop, and more as you climb. Headache, nausea or dizziness is more than slowness: rest and do not go higher.

payload.prompt: Group hike: should the fastest hiker set the pace?

scene.alt: A group of hikers strung out along a trail, with the slowest at the back.

explanation.correct: A group moves at the pace of its slowest member, and nobody gets left behind or waits alone out of earshot. That keeps everyone safe and together.
explanation.incorrect: Splitting a group leaves the slowest hiker alone, which is when people get lost or hurt. Keep everyone together at the slowest pace.

payload.prompt: A 20-pound pack slows your pace by roughly what percent compared to no pack?

explanation.correct: A 20-pound pack slows most hikers modestly, often somewhere around 5 to 15 percent, and more on steep or rough ground. Lighter packs are faster.
explanation.incorrect: Pack weight adds up. Twenty pounds might slow you around 10 percent on typical terrain, more on steep or rocky ground.

lessons.title: What moderate actually means
lessons.objective: You can explain why difficulty labels vary and what the class scale describes.

payload.prompt: Match the Yosemite class to the hiking challenge.

pairs.definition: Walking on a trail; no special skills needed
Simple scrambling on rough or off-trail ground; hands only for balance
Hands-on scrambling; a fall could be serious and some people want a rope
Exposed climbing where ropes are used; beyond hiking, needs training

distractorDefinitions: Running at high speed on a rocky summit

explanation.summary: The class scale goes from hike to scramble to climb. Class 3 is where hands matter and falls get serious. Treat the scale as a reading skill, not permission to try it.

statement.speaker: Her
statement.text: The trail is moderate on AllTrails but strenuous on the park site.

payload.question: What is she talking about?

options.text: Difficulty ratings differ by app and agency
Check miles and elevation gain, not labels
Moderate and strenuous mean the same thing

payload.translation: Difficulty ratings vary widely across apps. One's moderate is another's strenuous. Check objective metrics instead.

followUps.line: Look at miles and feet of gain, not the label alone.
followUps.why: The numbers tell you more than the subjective rating.

followUps.line: Ask locals or read trip reports for real feedback.
followUps.why: Recent experience beats any rating system.

followUps.line: Ask what moderate means to her before comparing.
followUps.why: Everyone's scale is different; clarify first.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Ratings are subjective. Asking 'What does moderate mean?' shows honesty, not ignorance.

payload.prompt: A trail labeled class 2 scramble means?

options.text: Hiking on a trail; safe for kids and dogs
Off-trail or rough ground with simple scrambling; hands only for balance
Hands-on scrambling with exposure; serious and high-risk

explanation.correct: Class 2 is simple scrambling on rough or off-trail ground; you might use a hand for balance. Falls are still possible, so know your limits and check current conditions.
explanation.incorrect: Class 2 is the first level of scramble: rough ground and some rock work, with hands used occasionally. It is not a plain trail, so plan for it.

payload.prompt: Which is most useful for comparing hikes objectively?

options.text: Elevation gain in feet and the class scale
Recent trip reports from other hikers

explanation.correct: Elevation gain and the class scale tell you how far you climb and what terrain you face, so they compare better than app labels. Check current conditions and official sources too.
explanation.incorrect: Distance alone misleads. Six miles with 100 feet feels easy; six miles with 3,000 feet feels hard. Gain plus class scale is more objective than a label.

payload.prompt: On a class 3 scramble, what is most important?

options.text: Testing hand and foot placement; fall risk is real
Carrying as much gear as possible

explanation.correct: Class 3 has exposure and fall risk. Test holds, move deliberately, and turn back if it feels beyond you. Beginners should build skills first or go with someone experienced.
explanation.incorrect: Class 3 demands attention and care. A fall can badly hurt you. Test every hold, move deliberately and respect the exposure. Rushing is how slips happen.

lessons.title: Trail, route, exposure, water
lessons.objective: You can read a description for red flags: routes, exposure, unreliable water.

payload.prompt: Trail description: 'Follow cairns across open rock for two miles.' Is this a trail or a route?

scene.alt: Bare rock with small stone cairns marking a path. No tread visible.

explanation.correct: No maintained tread, just cairns. That is a route. You navigate by rock, landmarks and markers, not a worn path.
explanation.incorrect: A trail has maintained tread; a route is a line across terrain marked by cairns or landmarks. This is a route, and navigation is part of the game.

payload.prompt: A guide says "Route, needs navigation." New to navigation, do you go solo?

options.text: Yes, with just a phone and a GPS track
Go with someone experienced, or take a navigation course first

explanation.correct: Routes demand navigation. A trail has tread; a route has only your judgment. Learn with an experienced partner or a course, and carry a paper map and compass.
explanation.incorrect: Routes need map and compass work, terrain reading and decision-making. Phones can fail, and footprints can lead anywhere. Learn with a mentor first.

payload.prompt: Complete the exposure idea.
payload.template: Exposure means {{what}} beside your route, where {{risk}}.

explanation.correct: Exposure is the vertical hazard: cliffs or steep drops beside the route. High exposure means a slip could be serious, so it asks for focus and care.
explanation.incorrect: Exposure is not about sun or mud. It is about how far and how hard you could fall, and it decides how much attention a section needs.

payload.prompt: Trail says: 'Water at mile 3 (seasonal). Do not rely on it.' Can you plan a 12-mile day using only that source?

scene.alt: A trail map with a water source marked at mile 3 labeled 'seasonal'.

explanation.correct: Seasonal means it may be dry when you go. The guide says do not rely on it. Bring all water or verify the source first via recent trip reports.
explanation.incorrect: When a guide says not to rely on water, believe it. Seasonal sources can be empty. Plan and carry what you need.

payload.prompt: Creek at 4 mi (reliable), spring at 8 mi (seasonal), dry for last 4. Carry?

options.text: One liter, there is water at mile 4
Enough to reach the creek, then refill and treat there without counting on the spring
Just download the route, water is always there
Two liters total, water is listed so it is reliable

explanation.correct: Carry enough for the dry first four miles. Refill and treat at the reliable creek at mile 4, and carry enough from there to the end. Seasonal springs can be dry, so do not count on one.
explanation.incorrect: Trust "reliable" and fill there, and treat the water. Do not count on "seasonal" sources, and carry what you need for the dry sections.
